event_subtitle: Exhibition Title: Diagrams of Memory: Interwoven Ontology
description:
Camille Ann Brewer lives and works in the City of Detroit, Michigan.  Through the process of textile construction, Brewer’s artwork intersects cartographic and photographic images that speak to specific spaces and time. Weaving together of physical place, memory with time is the core subject of this body of work.  

The artwork is built with time-period paper maps, which illustrate spatial geography and political territory; along with paper-collaged images of people, places and things, which tie directly to the history and human relationships in space.  In patterns that support the artwork’s theme, the two disparate paper elements are then woven together to create a serendipitous making and aesthetic experience.

combined_title: Comics Beyond Sight
description:
This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. 

Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. 

Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening.

View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

combined_title: Lila Kadaj Exhibition: Tic Tic
description:
Lila Kadaj received her MFA from Wayne State University. Her work has been shown at numerous institutions, including the Detroit Institute of Arts, the Cranbrook Art Museum, and the Arab American National Museum.  She spent nearly 27 years teaching art at Detroit Public schools.

Artist statement: “When looking at a beautiful flower.  It’s just itself.  Just there......no .....it does not proclaim its purpose for blooming is to make people happy. It just is. Like standing in front of an easel and painting........just is.......no matter......what proclamations may be concluded to sway the viewer. Same thing goes for fine art.  It’s not about I am a woman....it’s not about I am a first generation Arab American.....it’s not about being a child of trauma....it’s not about a member of my family being gunned down on the street....it’s about being born a painter.....standing in front of my easel and working to create a "Piece of Fine Art". Not standing on some soap box and expecting my words to somehow qualify my painting. It’s the painting, drawing or sculpture that must speak on its own.......on how the artist......via the intellect and muse uses the elements to create something distinct and first rate.   It can be quiet or loud. I see so much very weak work uplifted not for its quality but because it’s in fashion.”

event_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
combined_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
description:
Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union.

Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky  portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration.  

“For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.”
— Galina Lembersky, daughter

Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director.

Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky.

combined_title: Black Birth Joy: Announcing Lane Hall’s Fall Exhibition
description:
Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. 
 
Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. 

The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story.

The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan.

Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically  grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

description:
Small Works
Prints & Book Objects from Detroit 2020–2026

October 27 - November 19 
Public Reception: Friday, November 13 from 4:30-6pm.

Small Works was a print shop ran by Li Chen & Gerald Schulze, in Detroit, MI, from 2020–2026. Mariana Matos joined as the studio assistant, and later studio manager, in 2024. Over those six years, the business grew from an extension of their design practice to a community space that hosts more than 70 classes a year, open studio for the public, and year long funded fellowships that investigate practice in art and design related to the Book Arts. In 2026, they decided to expand community programming, and to accommodate this expansion closed Small Works, and formed Center for the Book Arts Detroit (BAD) which operates in the same space.

This exhibition is a eulogy for the former Small Works shop, and a celebration of all the people who made work here. It also serves to show what is possible as a community, when they share space and create work together. 

The work featured is a collection of things printed by Small Works, by their studiomates Diskette Press, the publisher Maamoul Press, and by the community that uses the space.

event_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

description:
RCGD Fall 2026 Seminar Series: Global Perspectives on Culture & Health, meets Mondays 3:30 to 5 at ISR Thompson 6050.

Global Perspectives on Culture and Health explores fundamental aspects of human life. Culture facilitates human interaction by providing meaning to lived experience. Accounting for culture in both theories and methods potentially advances the study of health by connecting the macro and micro levels of human experience. Yet, culture should be understood as dynamic and complex. It fundamentally shapes individuals and simultaneously is shaped by individuals. The importance of systematically attending to culture includes topics of values, language, immigration, and society.

Theories and methods that incorporate culture hold great potential for advancing the understanding of health outcomes and health trajectories in various global contexts.

The speakers for this series will focus on various aspects of culture and diverse groups living in the U.S. and across the globe to address the ways in which attending to culture helps clarify and overcome challenges to good health.

The Group Dynamics Seminar series is considered one of the longest running seminar series in the social sciences. It has been running uninterruptedly since it was founded by Kurt Lewin in the 1920’s in Berlin. The seminar series runs every semester on a theme chosen by faculty organizer/s who are affiliated with the Research Center for Group Dynamics at the Institute for Social Research. A very important feature of this seminar today is its interdisciplinary nature. Recent themes have included political polarization, evolution and human behavior, and cultural psychology.

event_title: Depressed Mothers and Rebellious Sons: Relationships in the History of American Mood Disorders
combined_title: Depressed Mothers and Rebellious Sons: Relationships in the History of American Mood Disorders: Laura Hirshbein, U-M
description:
The formal diagnosis of adult major depressive disorder emerged in the 1970s in the context of research with medication, though disagreement about whether children could experience depression was not resolved until the 1980s and 1990s. Many critics and scholars have interrogated the construction of psychiatric diagnosis in the United States. This talk will attend to the relationships that formed the backdrop in depression research, especially between depressed mothers and their rebellious sons. In the process of creating purportedly objective categories of illness, relationship dynamics were redefined as genetic propensity, while the brain was located as a value-neutral site, away from social context.

event_title: Easy to Collect, Costly to Bear: Mobile Money Taxation and  Network Spillovers in Tanzania
combined_title: Easy to Collect, Costly to Bear: Mobile Money Taxation and  Network Spillovers in Tanzania: Youssef Benzarti, University of California, Santa Barbara
event_subtitle: Youssef Benzarti, University of California, Santa Barbara
description: This paper provides evidence that a tax on mobile money transactions shrinks its base by an order of magnitude more than taxes on income or turnover do, that the base responds to whether it is taxed rather than to how much, and that the damage spreads through the payment network to users and payments the law never taxed. First, using the complete transaction records of Tanzania’s three largest providers around the introduction of a notched levy on person-to-person transfers and cash withdrawals in July 2021, we show that the levy reduces the volume of taxed transactions by 23 percent and their average value by 13 percent relative to untaxed transactions on the same platform, an elasticity with respect to the net-of-tax price of about 10. Second, we show that a cut of about 30 percent seven weeks later brings none of it back, nor do two further cuts, while the removal of the levy on transfers in 2023 does, slowly. Third, we document that relationships between senders and receivers survive at two-thirds the normal rate, that new ones form at less than half the pre-levy pace, and that senders stop rerouting activity around recipients who go quiet; none of these margins recovers when the tax rate falls. Fourth, we find that the levy reaches activity it does not tax, as wages paid into wallets fall by a fifth, and that senders of every size cut back by a similar share, whether or not they have a bank account. Fifth, we estimate that the levy destroys 47 cents of surplus for every shilling it raises, several times the cost of a value-added tax in comparable settings.

event_title: GLNT: Modular Character Sheaves and Monodromic Hecke Categories
combined_title: GLNT: Modular Character Sheaves and Monodromic Hecke Categories: Colton Sandvik (JHU)
description:
Abstract:  Character sheaves provide a geometric framework for studying characters of finite groups of Lie type. Introduced by Lusztig in the 1980s, they played a central role in the classification of irreducible complex representations of these groups and in the computation of their characters. Although the definition of character sheaves can be formulated with modular coefficients, much of Lusztig's characteristic-zero machinery breaks down in this setting.

In this talk, I will give a streamlined overview of the theory of character sheaves using modern language from categorical representation theory. From this perspective, categorical traces allow one to study character sheaves through monodromic Hecke categories. I will describe two models for these categories: a geometric categorification in terms of parity sheaves and an algebraic categorification in terms of Soergel bimodules. A key advantage of these models is that they are tightly controlled by p-Kazhdan–Lusztig combinatorics. This paves the way for a more algebraic study of modular character sheaves.

event_title: How plabic graphs describe weakly separated collections
combined_title: How plabic graphs describe weakly separated collections: Veronica Lang
description:
Two k-element subsets I,J of {1,2,…,n} are weakly separated if the sets I\J and J\I (when drawn on a circle with vertices 1,2,…,n) can be separated by a chord. A maximal weakly separated collection is a set of pairwise weakly-separated k-element subsets of {1,2,…,n} that is not contained in any larger set with this property. This definition gives rise to natural combinatorial questions: How big is a maximal weakly separated collection? How many are there? How are they related to each other?

I will outline how Oh, Posknikov, Speyer answered most of these questions via a bijection between maximal weakly separated collections in a positroid and move-equivalent plabic graphs. Along the way, we’ll meet some fun combinatorial objects related to plabic graphs including bounded affine permutations, Grassmann necklaces, positroids, and plabic tilings.

combined_title: Teresa Poggi Lecture on Italy and the Mediterranean World. “Signor Presidente:" Giorgia Meloni and the Italian Laboratory: Rachel Donadio, contributing writer at *The Atlantic*, former *The New York Times* Rome Bureau Chief and European Culture Correspondent
event_subtitle: Rachel Donadio, contributing writer at *The Atlantic*, former *The New York Times* Rome Bureau Chief and European Culture Correspondent
description:
In 2022, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni became the first far-right leader of Italy since Fascism and the first woman to ever lead the country. Four years later, Meloni has proven resilient, despite challenging economic indicators and after losing a referendum to limit the independence of the judiciary. A skillful politician, Meloni has deftly navigated between Italy’s commitments to the European Union and the country’s longtime strategic alliance with the United States, even as the Trump Administration has pushed to scale back NATO in Europe, causing confusion and distress in Europe’s halls of power.

   From Fascism to the personality-driven phenomenon of Silvio Berlusconi to the anti-system Five Star Movement, Italy has always been a political laboratory, a harbinger of political trends to come. With this lens, what larger lessons can we draw from Meloni’s leadership about the direction of Italy and Europe? Has Meloni normalized the far right or transformed it into a mainstream conservative movement? What are her most concrete accomplishments? As a study in power, what do we make of this small, blonde, fierce woman who insists on using the masculine form of address, “Signor Presidente”?
  
The annual Teresa Poggi Lecture on Italy and the Mediterranean World focuses on contemporary and historical issues related to the region. It is made possible by a generous gift from Stephanie and Sue Augustyniak in honor of their mother.
   
Rachel Donadio is a Paris-based writer, a contributing writer for *The Atlantic*, and a former Rome Bureau Chief and European Culture Correspondent for *The New York Times*. She regularly publishes textured profiles and features at the intersection of culture and politics, as well as literary criticism, and is a frequent contributor to *The New York Review of Books*. Donadio has reported from more than two dozen countries and interviewed heads of state and major cultural figures, including four Nobel Laureates in literature.
   
In her many years covering Italy, she has written on Giorgia Meloni’s culture wars, Curzio Malaparte, Nicola Gratteri when he was a leading Italian anti-Mafia prosecutor, former Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi, Gina Lollobrigida, Paolo Sorrentino, a rare book theft in Naples, why Italians gesticulate, Amalfi lemons, a family of centenarians in Sardinia, a Bangladeshi Cricket league in Rome, and the first non-Italian director of the Uffizi. She has also covered the Vatican and led *The New York Times* coverage of the conclave in which Pope Francis was elected.

Once the thriving capital of Imperial China, the city of Datong is now among the country’s most polluted cities, burdened by aging infrastructure and uncertain economic prospects. Mayor Geng Yanbo announces an ambitious plan to restore Datong to the cultural center it was 1,600 years ago. The Chinese Mayor offers remarkable access to a leader, and to a country, moving urgently toward an increasingly unstable future. It also allows audiences to draw their own conclusions about the promises and costs of the mayor’s project, while raising questions that continue to echo today.

event_title: Exploring the Mind | Pleasure, Desire, and Addiction in the Brain
combined_title: Exploring the Mind | Pleasure, Desire, and Addiction in the Brain: Kent Berridge James Olds Distinguished University Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience
event_subtitle: Kent Berridge James Olds Distinguished University Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience
description:
How is pleasure (‘liking’) different from desire (‘wanting’), and how are they generated by the brain? Answering those questions is crucial to understanding addiction, compulsivity, and many other aspects of human behavior. Our work at Michigan helped show that the brain’s mesolimbic dopamine system is not a pleasure ‘liking’ mechanism as was once thought, but rather only a motivational ‘wanting’ mechanism. Separate brain opioid hedonic hotspots generate feelings of ‘liking’.

In addiction, drug-induced sensitization of dopamine systems in vulnerable individuals can amplify ‘wanting’ to arguably compulsive levels, even when what is desired does not provide pleasure once obtained. A recent animal laboratory demonstration is ‘wanting what hurts:’ desiring experiences that give no pleasure at all, as a prototype of how addictive compulsion works. Incentive sensitization helps explain how addiction can create a vulnerability to relapse that persists despite sincere desire to quit, even long after drugs are no longer taken.

About the speaker: Kent Berridge is James Olds Distinguished University Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of Michigan. Research in Berridge’s lab has aimed for better answers to questions such as: How is pleasure (‘liking’) generated by the brain? How is desire (‘wanting’) generated by the brain? How does wanting something differ from liking it? And how does addiction become compulsive?

event_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
combined_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
description:
Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union.

Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky  portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration.  

“For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.”
— Galina Lembersky, daughter

Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director.

combined_title: Black Birth Joy: Announcing Lane Hall’s Fall Exhibition
description:
Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. 
 
Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. 

The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story.

The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan.

description:
Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically  grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

event_title: Small Works: Prints & Book Objects from Detroit, 2020–2026
combined_title: Small Works: Prints & Book Objects from Detroit, 2020–2026
description:
Small Works
Prints & Book Objects from Detroit 2020–2026

October 27 - November 19 
Public Reception: Friday, November 13 from 4:30-6pm.

Small Works was a print shop ran by Li Chen & Gerald Schulze, in Detroit, MI, from 2020–2026. Mariana Matos joined as the studio assistant, and later studio manager, in 2024. Over those six years, the business grew from an extension of their design practice to a community space that hosts more than 70 classes a year, open studio for the public, and year long funded fellowships that investigate practice in art and design related to the Book Arts. In 2026, they decided to expand community programming, and to accommodate this expansion closed Small Works, and formed Center for the Book Arts Detroit (BAD) which operates in the same space.

This exhibition is a eulogy for the former Small Works shop, and a celebration of all the people who made work here. It also serves to show what is possible as a community, when they share space and create work together. 

The work featured is a collection of things printed by Small Works, by their studiomates Diskette Press, the publisher Maamoul Press, and by the community that uses the space.

event_title: MCDB Dissertation Defense Seminar> The Regulation and Interactome of an H4K20-Specific Demethylase in Dosage Compensation of C. elegans
combined_title: MCDB Dissertation Defense Seminar> The Regulation and Interactome of an H4K20-Specific Demethylase in Dosage Compensation of C. elegans: Anati Alyaa Binti Azhar
description:
In species that use sex chromosomes to differentiate between its sexes, there is a difference in sex chromosome number and the number of gene copies which results in unequal gene dosage. In species that cannot tolerate this imbalance in gene dosage, the dosage compensation process is applied in which the gene expression levels between the two sexes are made equal. In mammals, female somatic cells (XX) have one X chromosome inactivated to equalize to the single X chromosome in male somatic cells (XY). In C. elegans, hermaphrodites (XX) downregulate both X chromosomes by half to equalize to the single X chromosome in their male counterparts (XO). 

Dosage compensation in C. elegans is conducted primarily by the Dosage Compensation Complex (DCC), a multimeric set of proteins including a CondensinIDC complex and several additional proteins that bind, compact and downregulate the X chromosomes in hermaphrodites. One of the non-condensin proteins in the DCC is DPY-21, a Histone 4 Lysine 20 (H4K20)- specific demethylase. DPY-21 binds to the hermaphroditic X chromosomes and converts H4K20 di-methylation (H4K20me2) into mono-methylation (H4K20me1). This results in the enrichment of the repressive H4K20me1 mark on the X and the transcriptional downregulation of the X chromosomes. Although DPY-21 is part of the DCC, it localizes to the X chromosomes at a later stage of embryogenesis and does not bind mitotic chromosomes, contrasting to the other DCC components. Additionally, DPY-21 has been shown to have a DCC-independent role in the germline where dosage compensation in unrequired. This drives the question of the regulation of DPY-21 and its interactors in addition to the DCC. 

The first part of my thesis is the characterization of DPY-21 regulation through phosphorylation. Using CRISPR/Cas9 site-directed mutagenesis, I generated a dpy-21 phosphomutant C.elegans strain by mutating the phosphosites of DPY-21 into Alanines to render them non-phosphorylatable. Through physiological assays, I found that the dpy-21 phosphomutant C. elegans strain has defects in embryogenesis and larval stages. In embryogenesis, the phosphomutations disrupts DPY-21’s localization to the X chromosomes and delays the enrichment of H4K20me1 to the X chromosomes. Through biochemical and imaging analysis, I demonstrate that the global levels of 4K20me1 is increased in the phosphomutant strain, suggesting that the mutant protein may be hyperactive. At the larval stages, the dpy-21 phosphomutant strain exhibits developmental delay and increased propensity to form dauers. These defects are resolved by  adulthood which implies that DPY-21’s activity is most critical in the embryonic and larval stages.

The second part of my work revealed novel interactors  of DPY-21. I conducted an immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS  ) on DPY-21 to establish its interacting partners and found the kinase SPK-1 to be a top interactor of DPY-21. In spk-1 mutants, there is delayed H4K20me1 enrichment on the X chromosomes in embryogenesis which ultimately results in disrupted H4K20me1 enrichment on the X chromosomes in adults. This shows that SPK-1 may regulate DPY-21 although this may be indirect. Taken together, my work has characterized a novel dpy-21 mutant for the field that leads to its hyperactivity in generating H4K20me1 globally as well as the novel interactor SPK-1 that may regulate DPY-21.

event_title: The Allocative Cost of War: A View to a Kill. . .ing of Productivity
combined_title: The Allocative Cost of War: A View to a Kill. . .ing of Productivity: Yuriy Gorodnichenko, University of California, Berkeley
event_subtitle: Yuriy Gorodnichenko, University of California, Berkeley
description: Why is war so economically costly? Our answer is that modern war lowers output not only by destroying productive factors, but also by making the surviving economy work less efficiently. Using uniquely comprehensive firm-level data collected during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, we document a dramatic collapse in allocative productivity in Ukraine. To sharpen identification and explore key mechanisms (including the role of war intensity, internal displacement, reallocation, and macroeconomic instability), we exploit spatial heterogeneity across Ukrainian districts and comparisons with Russian aggression in 2014 and the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. Our key policy implication is that restoring allocative efficiency–and preparing institutional arrangements that facilitate rapid reallocation in times of stress–is critical for sustaining economic capacity, defense, and national security.

event_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

event_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
combined_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.

event_title: EEB Tuesday Seminar Series - Multi-environment fitness landscapes suggest effectively endless adaptation
combined_title: EEB Tuesday Seminar Series - Multi-environment fitness landscapes suggest effectively endless adaptation: George Zhang, Marshall W. Nirenberg Collegiate Professor
event_subtitle: George Zhang, Marshall W. Nirenberg Collegiate Professor
description: Seminar Summary - The number of beneficial substitutions (N) required for an adapting population to reach a fitness peak is a fundamental but unknown parameter of evolution. We find that N increases linearly with the number of variable sites in empirical fitness landscapes, regardless of prior adaptation in another environment. Extrapolation suggests a minimal N of 10⁵ for typical prokaryotes and 10⁷ for mammals. In contrast, in highly rugged shuffled landscapes, N is markedly reduced, while fitness gains also shrink. The relatively smooth empirical landscapes therefore enable greater fitness gains while lengthening adaptive walks, rendering even local fitness peaks effectively unreachable because natural environments inevitably change. These results explain the persistence of fitness gains in long-term evolution experiments under constant environments and the widespread occurrence of beneficial mutations across species. They suggest that populations continuously adapt while remaining far from fitness optima, challenging the long-held view that adaptation culminates at fitness peaks.

combined_title: Kathy Beck & Vinson Lam, carillon
description:
Kathy Beck & Vinson Lam perform on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds.

Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

event_title: LRCCS Noon Lecture Series | From a 'Ton of Steel' to 'Another Province Overseas': Foreign and Diaspora Tourism to Mao-Era China
combined_title: LRCCS Noon Lecture Series | From a 'Ton of Steel' to 'Another Province Overseas': Foreign and Diaspora Tourism to Mao-Era China: Gavin Healy, Columbia University
description:
Please note: This lecture will be held in person and virtually on Zoom. If you would like to attend via Zoom, registration is required. Once you've registered, joining information will be sent to your email. Register for the Zoom webinar at: https://myumi.ch/gk19J

In the early years of the People’s Republic of China, state tourism officials saw sightseeing as a form of public diplomacy, but noted also that they could earn as much from hosting just one Soviet tourist as they could from exporting a ton of steel. At the same time, the vast majority of visitors to China during the Mao years came from China’s diaspora, which officials referred to as “another province overseas” that could contribute to the economic and political foundations of the new nation. This talk will examine the challenges faced by China’s state tourism officials in promoting foreign and diaspora tourism as a form of public diplomacy and economic development from the founding of the PRC to the Cultural Revolution.

Gavin Healy is a center associate of the Lieberthal-Rogel Center for Chinese Studies at the University of Michigan and has taught Chinese history at Columbia University and the State University of New York. He is the author of *A Guide to Mao’s China: Showing the Nation to Foreign Guests* (Cornell University Press, 2026). His work appears in *20th Century China*, *Modern China*, and the *Journal of Contemporary History*.

event_title: An Introduction to Singularities in Positive Characteristic
combined_title: An Introduction to Singularities in Positive Characteristic: Zander Hill
description:
Singularity theory is the study of how far regular local rings are from being smooth. In general, even if a ring fails to be smooth, it can still have many nice properties that allow arguments to go through: reduced, normal, CM, Gorenstein, among others. 

However, there are some types of singularities in complex geometry whose definitions break down in positive characteristic. They may rely on analytic techniques, or secretly divide by n!. In positive characteristic we then need different methods to define them. 

We'll talk about how these properties are defined in terms of the Frobenius map, why this map contains information about singularities, and how one can meaningfully compare singularity types in characteristic zero or positive characteristic.

event_title: CM-AMO Seminar | Measuring Gravity by Dropping Atoms
combined_title: CM-AMO Seminar | Measuring Gravity by Dropping Atoms: Xuejian Wu (Rutgers University)
description:
Leveraging the nature of quantum phenomena, quantum technologies are advancing rapidly in computing, communication, and sensing. Quantum inertial sensors based on light-pulse atom interferometry are powerful tools for precision measurements, navigation, geoscience, and civil engineering. By contrast to classical sensors, atom interferometers use photon momentum to coherently split and recombine matter waves. Since the laser wavelength precisely determines photon momentum, atom interferometers are highly accurate and have demonstrated unprecedented sensitivity and stability. In this talk, I will present compact and versatile atom interferometers for measuring the local gravity field and sensing multi-axis accelerations and rotations. With simplicity and sensitivity, our technology paves the way for deploying quantum sensors in field applications.

Bio: Dr. Xuejian Wu joined the Physics Department at Rutgers University-Newark in January 2021. From 2015 to 2020, he was a postdoctoral scholar in the Physics Department at the University of California, Berkeley. In January 2015, Dr. Wu received his PhD from Tsinghua University, China. Dr. Wu serves as an associate editor for Optics Express and an editorial board member for Atoms.

event_title: Colloquium: Heat, wave, and Schrödinger dynamics of Gibbs measures
combined_title: Colloquium: Heat, wave, and Schrödinger dynamics of Gibbs measures: Bjoern Bringmann, Caltech
description:
Gibbs measures were first introduced in statistical mechanics, where they have been used to describe statistical equilibria of physical systems. In recent years, there has been significant interest in the dynamics of Gibbs measures under heat, wave, and Schrödinger equations. In the first part of the talk, we will discuss the invariance of Gibbs measures under the cubic nonlinear wave equation. In the second part of the talk, we will then discuss the global well-posedness of the stochastic Yang--Mills heat flow. 

The talk is based on joint works with Y. Deng, A. Nahmod, and H. Yue, and separately with S. Cao, M. Hairer, and W. Zhao.

combined_title: Robotics Department Seminar Series: Towards Personalized AI Assistants: Reid Simmons
description:
Robotics Department Seminar Series (https://robotics.umich.edu/events/robotics-seminar-series/)
Speaker: Reid Simmons, Research Professor, Robotics and Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University
Title: "Towards Personalized AI Assistants"
Date: Tuesday, November 2, 2026
Time: 4:00 - 5:00 pm ET
Location: FRB 2300 + Zoom
Zoom Link: https://myumi.ch/9JjZ7
Meeting ID: 910 7047 6728
Passcode: 575785

Abstract: As the population ages, the need grows for AI agents to assist people to remain independent for longer.  Older adults are typically set in their ways, so AI agents should adapt to their ways of doing things, rather than the other way around.  To that end, we are exploring various approaches to learning to personalize assistive agents, including the use of bandit algorithms, foundational models, neuro-symbolic architectures, and theory of mind.  This talk will present our approaches and results in several assistive areas, including meal preparation and exercise coaching, as well as work in learning policies from humans.  Much of the research is being supported by AI-CARING, an NSF-sponsored Institute devoted to developing AI technologies to help older adults with cognitive and physical decline remain in their homes.

Speaker Bio: Dr. Reid Simmons is a Research Professor in the Robotics Institute and Computer Science Department at Carnegie Mellon University.  He received his PhD from MIT in Artificial Intelligence, and since coming to CMU in 1988, his research has focused on developing self-reliant robots that can autonomously operate over extended periods of time in unknown, unstructured environments, and on human-robot social interaction, especially non-verbal communication through affect, proxemics, motion, and gesture.  He is co-PI and Research Director for the NSF-sponsored AI-CARING Institute.  Dr. Simmons is an author of over 250 publications on AI, Robotics, and Human-Robot Interaction and has graduated 25 PhD students.  He previously served as a Program Director at the National Science Foundation, where he oversaw the National Robotics Initiative and initiated the Smart and Autonomous Systems program.  In 2018, Dr. Simmons helped found the first-in-the-nation standalone undergraduate major in Artificial Intelligence and currently serves as its program director.  He is a Fulbright Scholar, a Fellow of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence, a Senior Member of IEEE, and was an ONR Summer Faculty Fellow in 2022.

combined_title: FYRST Workshops 2026 - 2027: FYRST Workshop
description:
If you are only seeing one workshop, please SIGN-IN and refresh the Sessions page! If still having issues, click this link. 
First-Year Relationship and Sexuality Talk (FYRST) is a required, in-person, and peer-facilitated workshop that came directly from feedback and listening sessions with current University of Michigan students. Our goal is to create an accessible, supportive space for student-driven conversations where all identities and experiences are welcomed and in which students can build skills and tools around identifying goals and values and then communicate effectively about those. Workshops will be offered at multiple locations and times throughout the fall semester, so please sign up for the workshop that works for you!! First-Year Relationship Sexuality Talk (FYRST) FAQ:
“How many workshops do I have to sign up for?”
You only need to sign up for 1 workshop. Attending 1 workshop will fulfill the requirement for the training. 
“I see that there is more than one session, does it matter which one I sign up for?”
It generally does not matter which workshop you sign up for. There will be a few that are designated for specific groups such as transfer students or for students looking for accommodations. If you do not fit these groups please try to save these workshops for those that do and you are free to choose among any of the other workshops. 
“Is this workshop required?”
This workshop is required for all transfer and first-year students at the University of Michigan.
“I’ve experienced harm around relationships or sexual experiences in the past and I am worried that attending this workshop may be harmful for me.” 
Our team is aware that students who are coming into the university that have experienced harm in the past. Our workshop is specifically designed to respect and validate the experiences of survivors and has been carefully constructed to avoid any specific descriptions of violence and focus instead on themes of empowerment, communication, and boundary setting. However, if you still have concerns about programming and would like to request alternative programming, please feel free to reach out at SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.
“What if I struggle to learn in a presentation setting? I’m an active learner.”
Our workshop is built to meet a variety of learning styles, including time for self-reflection, small group sharing, and resources to take with you to work through on your own time! This workshop is meant to be interactive and inclusive. 
“Can I request accommodations?”
We considered accessibility in creating this workshop and selecting the locations in which the workshops are help. However, we recognize many places at the University are inaccessible and we've set an * next to workshops that are on the first floor and lack stairs. These workshops also will have a presentation (other workshops we do not) and are a good fit for those who might need a large font. Please sign up for those if you feel that accommodations would assist you and reach out to SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu if you are concerned or have questions. 
“I missed my workshop, what should I do ?”
Our team tracks attendance at each workshop by having participants swipe in with their MCard. If you are not able to attend the workshop you signed up for, our team will continue to send reminder emails until you have completed a workshop. In this case, please sign up for another workshop as soon as you can as the workshop is required and may fill up especially near the end of the semester. No need to contact SAPAC unless you are not able to reschedule. 
“I have had gender-based violence training before, can I get this requirement waived?”
As this workshop was designed with University of Michigan student feedback in mind, our workshop is unique to the UM community. Our curriculum focuses on individualized reflection and because of its interactive nature, each workshop will be unique to the people attending. Although we are excited you already have familiarity with the subject, this workshop is required for every first year and transfer student. 
“I’m a commuter/non-traditional student, do I still have to attend?"
Yes, this workshop is required for every first-year and transfer student - not only do we want every student to benefit from having this time to connect with peers, but we also want to make sure your peers benefit from what you bring to our community. If you have any concerns or questions about being able to participate, please contact SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.
“I still have questions! Who should I contact?"
Please contact us at SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.

event_title: Global Wellposedness for the Hele-Shaw Problem with Point Injection
combined_title: Global Wellposedness for the Hele-Shaw Problem with Point Injection: Zhengjun(Jasper) Liang
description: We study the two-dimensional Hele-Shaw problem with point injection for star-shaped domains. We reduce the system to a nonlocal parabolic equation of the interface, and for arbitrary Lipschitz initial interface away from the source, we prove global well-posedness of the interface equation in a strong sense. We also introduce a viscosity-solution framework for the interface equation and relate it to the classical viscosity theory for the Hele-Shaw problem.

combined_title: Teddy Thompson: Presented by The Ark
description:
“Buoyant, soulful” –Billboard 

Beloved London-born, Brooklyn-based singer/songwriter Teddy Thompson has returned with the exquisitely crafted Never Be The Same, his first collection of original material since 2020. Across ten tracks, Thompson refines his craft via an exploration of music’s enduring preoccupations — love, longing, and the uneasy passage of time.

This album wasn’t built upon a grand narrative. There was no self-imposed exile, no forced reinvention. Instead, it is centered around an exhortation that is threaded through the songs like a refrain: “Never Be The Same,” its title only revealing itself to Thompson after he’d completed the recording.

“It’s a phrase that, unconsciously, I used twice. And when I saw it on the page, I realized, this is the message of this album,” says Thompson. “Don’t ever be the same. Change. Grow! Even when the sentiment is, woe is me, I’ll never recover after that love or loss. The message is still, change. Don’t get too comfortable. Everything is temporary, so evolve or perish!”

This pull and tension between comfort and change runs quietly throughout Never Be The Same, Thompson’s 11th album, which was produced by renowned Grammy Award–winning musician/producer David Mansfield. At the core is Thompson’s longstanding commitment to songwriting as a form, inspired by early influences like Chuck Berry, Hank Williams, and Crowded House, as well as the towering figures of the craft — Bob Dylan, Leonard Cohen, The Beatles, and, certainly, his parents, British folk icons Richard and Linda Thompson.

Ultimately, Never Be The Same is an album about steady evolution, a suite of deeply considered, carefully constructed songs rooted in lived experience. If there is a message, it’s that change is not only inevitable but essential — even when you’d rather stay exactly where you are.

event_title: Medicine Needs Poetry: Reimagining Healthcare, Healing & Human Connection
combined_title: Medicine Needs Poetry: Reimagining Healthcare, Healing & Human Connection: Janna Lopez
description:
Poetry is one of humankind's oldest forms of expression. Expressive writing is an evidence-based strategy for reducing burnout among healthcare workers, and more broadly for making meaning of experiences that are complex, uncertain, and difficult to name. This
 interdisciplinary workshop explores poetry as a modality for improving individual health, care systems, and healing, and explores how poetry invites reflection, deepens attention, and nurtures consideration of the full human experience within healthcare. Lead
 by Janna Lopez, MFA, Creighton University School of Medicine's Poet in Residence, this workshop will ask participants to consider how poetic expression can support personal well-being, strengthen relationships between patients and caregivers, and contribute
 to more reflective, compassionate, and human-centered cultures of care. Participants will be introduced to
Poetic Intelligence as a framework for cultivating powers of observation, curiosity, expression, self-compassion, and meaning-making.  Everyone is encouraged to attend - no prior creative writing or poetry experience is required. 



Janna Lopez, MFA, is the inaugural Poet-in-Residence at Creighton University School of Medicine, and the first to hold such a position in the US.  She works with students, healthcare professionals, educators, and healthcare teams to make poetry accessible
 as a tool for navigating complex human experiences. She is the author of Medicine Needs Poetry: An Open Invitation to Cultivate More Self-Care & Compassion Through Words. An award-winning writer, educator, and speaker, Lopez previously served as a Santa
 Fe Poet Laureate. Her work advocates for the humanities as an essential component of health, education, and human connection.

description:
Camille Ann Brewer lives and works in the City of Detroit, Michigan.  Through the process of textile construction, Brewer’s artwork intersects cartographic and photographic images that speak to specific spaces and time. Weaving together of physical place, memory with time is the core subject of this body of work.  

The artwork is built with time-period paper maps, which illustrate spatial geography and political territory; along with paper-collaged images of people, places and things, which tie directly to the history and human relationships in space.  In patterns that support the artwork’s theme, the two disparate paper elements are then woven together to create a serendipitous making and aesthetic experience.

combined_title: Comics Beyond Sight
description:
This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. 

Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. 

Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening.

View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

combined_title: Lila Kadaj Exhibition: Tic Tic
description:
Lila Kadaj received her MFA from Wayne State University. Her work has been shown at numerous institutions, including the Detroit Institute of Arts, the Cranbrook Art Museum, and the Arab American National Museum.  She spent nearly 27 years teaching art at Detroit Public schools.

Artist statement: “When looking at a beautiful flower.  It’s just itself.  Just there......no .....it does not proclaim its purpose for blooming is to make people happy. It just is. Like standing in front of an easel and painting........just is.......no matter......what proclamations may be concluded to sway the viewer. Same thing goes for fine art.  It’s not about I am a woman....it’s not about I am a first generation Arab American.....it’s not about being a child of trauma....it’s not about a member of my family being gunned down on the street....it’s about being born a painter.....standing in front of my easel and working to create a "Piece of Fine Art". Not standing on some soap box and expecting my words to somehow qualify my painting. It’s the painting, drawing or sculpture that must speak on its own.......on how the artist......via the intellect and muse uses the elements to create something distinct and first rate.   It can be quiet or loud. I see so much very weak work uplifted not for its quality but because it’s in fashion.”

event_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
combined_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
description:
Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union.

Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky  portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration.  

“For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.”
— Galina Lembersky, daughter

Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director.

Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky.

combined_title: Black Birth Joy: Announcing Lane Hall’s Fall Exhibition
description:
Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. 
 
Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. 

The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story.

The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan.

combined_title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s: American Home Cooking
description:
Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically  grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

combined_title: Like the flowing river: An exhibition by Tomoyuki Ueno
description:
Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience.

This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor.

*The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

Small Works
Prints & Book Objects from Detroit 2020–2026

October 27 - November 19 
Public Reception: Friday, November 13 from 4:30-6pm.

Small Works was a print shop ran by Li Chen & Gerald Schulze, in Detroit, MI, from 2020–2026. Mariana Matos joined as the studio assistant, and later studio manager, in 2024. Over those six years, the business grew from an extension of their design practice to a community space that hosts more than 70 classes a year, open studio for the public, and year long funded fellowships that investigate practice in art and design related to the Book Arts. In 2026, they decided to expand community programming, and to accommodate this expansion closed Small Works, and formed Center for the Book Arts Detroit (BAD) which operates in the same space.

This exhibition is a eulogy for the former Small Works shop, and a celebration of all the people who made work here. It also serves to show what is possible as a community, when they share space and create work together. 

The work featured is a collection of things printed by Small Works, by their studiomates Diskette Press, the publisher Maamoul Press, and by the community that uses the space.

combined_title: Fore-Site (Phase 3): The Stamps Gallery Pillar Project
description:
From September 2025 through December 2026, Stamps Gallery is partnering in a curatorial collaboration with two Southeast Michigan-based, artist-run project spaces led by Stamps alumni: C.Y.N.K. Studios, directed by Sally Clegg (Lecturer III and Student Exhibition Coordinator, MFA ’20) and Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20); and Sometimes Space, directed by Nathan Byrne (Lecturer I, MFA ’21). Each space hosts dozens of artists annually for exhibitions, performances, and events, fostering experimental work and building community. For this project, Byrne, Clegg, and Narula have been commissioned to reimagine the pillars on Division Street that flank the gallery. In response, they’ve curated six artists to create new work for the pillars over three cycles:

Phase 1 (September 12 - December 12) artists: Amelia Burns (Cranbrook MFA ’23) and Erin McKenna (MFA ’20)
Phase 2 (January 12 - August 12) artists: Sally Clegg (MFA ’20) and Kim Karlsrud (MFA ’20)
Phase 3 (September 11 - December 11) artists: Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20) and Nathan Byrne (MFA ’21)
Phase 3 

Curated by Sometimes Space: Abhishek Narula (entry pillar)
Curated by CYNK Studios: Nathan Byrne (courtyard pillar)

Artist Statements/Bios

Abhishek Narula, Compressions 
Compressions is an installation comprised of 416 industrial-grade zip ties, cinched around the entry pillar of the Stamps Gallery. The pillar measures roughly 110 inches in circumference, requiring two ties per row to wrap around it, resulting in 208 rows. The humble zip tie, typically used to hang and bind other material, is relegated to its functional properties rendering it unprepossessing and easily dismissed. The zip tie in this installation, instead serves as an object of aesthetic possibility, pulling it out of its usual background role to become the work itself. The resulting composition is a proposal to dwell, to slow down, and to simply see the pillar.

Abhishek Narula is an artist, designer, and educator who works across sculpture, installation, sound, and video. His practice takes the form of interventions, working with what is already present. He reorients and disrupts objects and sites in order to open up formal possibilities and poetic experiences within the familiar. He is influenced by physical and digital infrastructural systems that sustain modern life and culture. His work treats this ambience itself as raw material for aesthetic inquiry, exploring themes of labor, precarity, temporality and the sublime. Narula earned his MFA in Studio Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and his MS/BS in Electrical Engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His work has been exhibited at national and international venues such as the Ammerman Center for Arts and Technology, Science Gallery Detroit, Speculum Artium Media Festival in Slovenia, New Media Caucus (NMC), WaveFarm, The Boulder Public Library, The Hyde Park Art Center, Sector 2337 Art Gallery & Printing Press, Tangible Embedded Interaction (TEI), International Symposium of Electronic Arts (ISEA), among others. He is a Robotics Systems Designer and Lecturer in the Robotics Department at the University of Michigan. Website / Instagram

Nathan Byrne, Equally To Be Loved
Equally To Be Loved is an image / object scaled to and installed upon the courtyard pillar of Stamps Gallery. The image is of a spontaneous sculpture made in 2017 during the first day of an artist residency at the Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program. The sculpture was constructed in a storage container studio using 14 discrete objects that were in his studio upon entry. For Byrne, this work embodies the energy and spirit of a studio at the start of a particularly fecund period of making. This work speaks to the artist’s interest in embodied experience of space, archival and site responsiveness, as well as his ongoing engagement with found materials. Byrne considers this project to be a far-flung sequel to his MFA thesis exhibition Equally Empty, which was shown at Stamps Gallery in 2021. Equally To Be Loved is the second line of the Buddhist mantra from which both titles are derived.

Nathan Byrne is an artist / educator / curator currently based in Detroit, MI. Through spatial and archive responsive projects, he reimagines, and explores within frameworks such as language, the passage of time, and contemplation. Intrigued by the potential of conveying phenomenal, transformative, and emotive states through materiality, process, and placement, he negotiates the pliability of the viewer’s encounters with objects and environments. Byrne holds an MFA in Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and a BA in Studio Art and Art History from San Francisco State University. He has been a Lecturer at Stamps School of Art & Design since the Fall of 2022. His work is exhibited widely nationally and he is a recipient of the VSC Fellowship at Vermont Studio Center. He has been awarded numerous artist residencies including Anderson Ranch Arts Center, I-Park, KHN Center for the Arts, Prairie Ronde, Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program, and Rockland Woods. event_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

combined_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.

event_title: HET Brown Bag Seminar | Suppressed Quantum Effects of Weakly Coupled Waves
combined_title: HET Brown Bag Seminar | Suppressed Quantum Effects of Weakly Coupled Waves: Kevin Zhou (Berkeley)
description: Searches for axion dark matter and gravitational waves are rapidly expanding, with new experiments deploying quantum sensing techniques to reach unprecedented precision. But does one need to account for the quantum nature of the axion or GW itself? I will exhibit two severe obstructions. First, realistic detectors cannot resolve the fundamental modes of a field; instead they couple to coarse-grained "effective" modes, which often washes out nonclassical effects. Second, all nonclassical effects are suppressed by extra powers of the weak coupling, making them much harder to detect than the waves themselves. This suppression applies to all observables, including quadrature and number statistics, entanglement, and decoherence, and rules out many proposed methods to detect the quantization of gravity.

description:
Respondent: Pauline Jones, U-M

What explains the rise and resilience of religious movements in historically secular contexts? Pious Politics (Cambridge University Press, 2025) investigates this question through the case of Islamist mobilization in Turkey. Drawing on two years of archival research and ethnographic fieldwork in formal and clandestine religious networks in Turkey, Ozgen shows that the Turkish Islamists captured the state by developing a popular, well-organized movement that rallied the masses and built vigorous political parties. But an equally formative, if not more significant, factor was the cultural groundwork Islamists laid through a quiet, gradual, and remarkably robust model of mobilization. Leveraging this groundwork, Islamists taught people to act politically in everyday life—situating personal choices about dress, speech, comportment, and social relations against a particular sociopolitical worldview. Pious Politics advances debates across political, historical, and cultural sociology, as well as scholarship on Islam and the Middle East.

event_title: Student DGT: From Killing Homotopy to Complex Cobordism
combined_title: Student DGT: From Killing Homotopy to Complex Cobordism: Ajay Srinivasan
description: Computing the homotopy groups of spheres has been a central motivator in algebraic topology for decades. In this talk I’d like to unravel one approach to this problem, built around the idea of killing homotopy groups, and see how far it takes us. I’ll begin with the classical story of killing homotopy, as it appears in Serre’s finiteness theorem for the homotopy groups of spheres. Then I’ll turn this trick into an industrial-grade construction: the Adams-Novikov spectral sequence, a machine for computing stable homotopy groups. We will redeem this unraveling into a spectral sequence by an explicit description of the cobordism ring of complex manifolds! Through this identification I'll sketch a remarkable relationship between cobordism, cohomology, and formal group laws. This relationship forms the bedrock of chromatic homotopy theory, which organizes periodic phenomena in stable homotopy groups that I will briefly discuss at the end.

description:
There is a well-known obstruction distinguishing an action of a finite group G on a derived category from a mere identification of G with a subgroup of the group of autoequivalences. I will first explain how to extend this distinction to a family of categories and, in the case of K3 surfaces, how to use stability conditions to completely control this construction. 

As one example, this leads to a construction of non-commutative abelian surfaces (categories deformation-equivalent to derived categories of abelian surfaces) in exactly as much generality as one could reasonably hope for. The applications include the construction of every polarised Hyperkaehler variety of Kummer type from a moduli space.

This is based on joint work with Alex Perry, Laura Pertusi and Xiaolei Zhao.

event_title: Exploratory Optimal Reinsurance under the Mean-Variance Criterion
combined_title: Exploratory Optimal Reinsurance under the Mean-Variance Criterion: Austin Riis-Due, Waterloo
description:
This paper proposes a Reinforcement Learning (RL) approach to the optimal reinsurance problem
when the insurer faces uncertainty about the insurance claim dynamics. To this end, we first formulate
an exploratory version of the problem as a relaxed stochastic control problem. Within a broad class of
parametric retention functions and general risk loading functions, we derive the closed-form equilibrium
policy under the continuous-time mean-variance criterion. This is achieved through a formal verification
theorem and solving classical solutions of a system of exploratory extended Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman
(EEHJB) equations. We then establish a policy iteration theorem, showing that starting from any timeand state-homogeneous policy, policy iteration converges to the derived equilibrium policy. Next, we
develop a martingale orthogonality theorem, which serves as the foundation of our RL algorithm. The
algorithm is evaluated through simulation studies and real data from the U.S. National Flood Insurance
Program. Results demonstrate that the RL approach effectively learns unknown claim distributions,
tracks unobserved changes in claim dynamics and produces higher insurer surplus trajectories than the
maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) approach while simultaneously exhibiting greater robustness to
the choice of training window.

event_title: Probability and Analysis: Strongly log-concave measures and lattices
combined_title: Probability and Analysis: Strongly log-concave measures and lattices: Brayden Letwin (UWashington)
description:
Let L be a lattice in R^n. Suppose that L has the property that the determinant of every non-zero sublattice L' of L is larger than one. We prove that there exists a symmetric random vector X on R^n with a smooth, strictly positive density f on R^n simultaneously enjoying the following two properties: a) f is strongly log-concave; b) X + L is uniform on R^n/L.

Moreover, the existence of such a density f on R^n characterizes this determinant condition imposed on L. This construction connects several problems in lattice theory to established results in convex geometry. We discuss a range of applications. This is joint work with Victor Reis and Thomas Rothvoss.

description:
I will talk about two loosely related results about
dense subgroups of compact groups, one with Sven Sandfeldt,
the other with Michael Larsen.  The first concerns local rigidity
of group actions, the second spectral gaps.  I hope to explain
some questions that arise in this context and invite people
to think about them.

event_title: Student AIM Seminar: Instrument-Aware Diffusion for Solar Magnetogram Reconstruction
combined_title: Student AIM Seminar: Instrument-Aware Diffusion for Solar Magnetogram Reconstruction: Ian Augsburger
description: Historical scientific archives often contain observations of lasting value that were acquired with lower-resolution instruments than those available today. Solar magnetograms provide a motivating example: the Michelson Doppler Imager (MDI) aboard the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO) recorded decades of solar activity before the higher-resolution Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) became available. We develop a generative framework that first learns how modern observations are transformed by an older instrument, uses this transformation to construct paired training data, and then trains a conditional diffusion model to reverse the loss of resolution. A scalable multiscale U-Net and DPM++ sampler generate multiple modern-quality reconstructions from each historical observation. More broadly, this provides a general strategy for connecting scientific archives across generations of instruments.
